name: Social-engineering scenario analysis
identify_givens: A detailed narrative/transcript of a scam: an attacker (phishing email, vishing phone call, fake charity/company) contacts a named victim, with quoted attacker lines, victim actions (clicking, entering credentials, opening attachments, confirming with BankID/PayPal), and the final state of what was revealed or executed. Often mentions public data sources the attacker combined (hitta.se, hemnet.se) and lookalike domains (paypa1.com, gmaill.com).
identify_target: (a) Identify ~3 manipulation strategies, name the human trait each exploits, and quote/mention the exact scenario lines supporting each (1 point per element); (b) state concretely what the attacker obtained; (c) give two examples of what the attacker can do now (follow-on attacks).
identify_keywords: quote or mention the parts of the scenario
what can the attacker do now
strategy_name: Strategy-trait-quote triangulation, then concrete harvest and follow-on attacks

algorithm.detail: Read the transcript and list every distinct manipulation move: impersonation of an organization/role, claimed affiliations, time pressure, appeals to suffering/helping, name-dropping neighbors or colleagues, friendly banter, plausible artifacts (order numbers, hold music, lookalike domains, 'we never send attachments' disclaimers).

algorithm.action: Map each move to a named strategy
algorithm.detail: Label each move with the course's strategy vocabulary: pretext-trappings of the role, pretext-putting victim into a victim or helper role (altercasting), urgency/rush, threat/fear, peer pressure/social proof, rapport/empathy/light banter.

For each strategy name the exploited trait: attribution/trust (role trappings), reduced cognitive ability under time pressure or fear, desire to be helpful/cooperative and not deviate from social expectations (peer pressure, helper role), people agree to more from someone they like (rapport), reactance (fixing a created problem).

For each strategy-trait pair, quote or precisely reference the scenario line: e.g. 'the payment of SEK 9999 has already come through' for fear; the grading rubric gives 1 point each for strategy, trait, and quote, so deliver all three explicitly.

Enumerate only what the transcript shows the attacker actually obtained: opened/executed attachment, credentials entered on the lookalike site, full personnummer/PII, confirmed BankID/PayPal transfer, phone number. Do not list things not evidenced in the story.

Provide two realistic next steps consistent with the harvest: malware in the attachment (ransomware, credential stealers) even if payment is refused; account takeover if no 2FA; initiating a real transaction the victim confirms; identity theft at services where a personnummer alone suffices as authentication; credential reuse on other sites.

variations.name: Callback phishing (vishing) instead of inbound link
variations.detail: In 'I'll be (call-)back' the email contains no link or attachment and the victim is lured into calling the attacker's number; the attack then happens live by phone with the 'attachment' arriving later. Adapt by treating hold music, the 'we never include links' disclaimer, and marketing-style email as role trappings, and note the extra harvest channel: spoken personnummer digits completed via hitta.se lookup. Trap: don't claim the initial email itself carried malware — the attachment comes in the follow-up 'cancellation form' mail.

variations.name: Charity/donation scam with social proof
variations.detail: In 'Donation matching' the lever is peer pressure ('the Ericssons and the Smiths have already donated') plus urgency (matching deadline 'before Lucia, tomorrow') and a helper-role pretext ('people are displaced and suffering'). Adapt by naming social proof and altercasting instead of fear; the harvest is PayPal credentials via a lookalike redirect (stockholmhelps.paypa1.com) plus a downloaded file. Trap: notice the '1' for 'l' domain substitution as part of the pretext.

variations.name: Grading granularity of part (a)
variations.detail: Both sittings award 9 points as 3 strategies x (strategy 1p + trait 1p + quote 1p). Giving strategies without the trait or without a quote forfeits two-thirds of the points; giving more than 3 is fine as sample answers list 4-5 acceptable options. Adapt by always writing full triples.

variations.name: What-counts-as-harvest trap in part (b)
variations.detail: Official solutions mark part (b) correct if at least one true gain is mentioned and no incorrect ones — so over-claiming (e.g. 'attacker got the money' before the BankID confirmation, or 'got the password' when only digits were given) loses the point. Adapt by listing only gains explicitly shown in the scenario's final state.

example_problem: Social engineering - I'll be (call-)back: Eric receives an 'Order confirmation' email from no-reply@northernfitness.se for a SEK 9999 two-year gym membership he never ordered, paid via 'his' Klarna account; the no-reply mail states 'we will never include links or attachments' and invites him to call customer service about friskvårdsbidrag reimbursement. Eric calls, hears hold music ('The Eye of the Tiger'), and 'Arnold' chats about friends pushing fitness and colleagues talking about carbs, then asks for Eric's name and last four digits of his personnummer 'to confirm it's really you' (Arnold completes it via a hitta.se lookup). Arnold says the payment has already come through, offers cancellation within 2 weeks, and emails a cancellation form; Eric opens the attachment, fills it in, scans a QR code and confirms a BankID request 'Northern Fitness Reimbursement - SEK 9999'. 8a: Identify 3 strategies used by the social engineer, for each the human trait exploited, and quote the parts of the scenario you refer to. 8b: What did the attacker get? 8c: Give two examples of what the attacker can do now.

example_steps.work: Inventory the moves: fake order-confirmation email with order/account numbers and marketing tone; hold music; 'we never include links or attachments' disclaimer; claim that the SEK 9999 payment 'has already come through'; banter about pushy friends and colleagues' carb talk; a created problem (unwanted membership) that Arnold 'fixes'.

Name strategies (official sample answers): 1) pretext: trappings of the role; 2) threat/fear; 3) building rapport/showing empathy/light banter; 4) pretext: put into victim role (fixing a created problem).

Attach traits: role trappings exploit attribution/trust; fear exploits reduced cognitive ability; rapport exploits that people agree to more from someone they like; the victim-role pretext exploits reactance/altercasting.

Quote evidence: trappings - 'plausible story, no links or attachments, statement about links or attachments, marketing style, on-hold music'; fear - 'saying the payment of SEK 9999 has already come through'; rapport - 'talking about people pushing fitness or diets'; victim role - 'creating and pretending to fix a problem'. Any three full triples earn 9/9.

8b official answer: the attacker got Eric to open a file attached to an e-mail, confirm a money transfer with BankID, the full personnummer, and the phone number (one correct gain suffices, no incorrect ones).

8c official answer: hidden malware in the attachment, e.g. ransomware or attempts to get login credentials, even if Eric does not authorize the transfer; get the money if he has authorized it; mount identity-theft attacks at places that do not verify a personnummer with any other factor of authentication.
